country.lede: What is Canada’s central bank dealing with right now, and what will it most likely do at its next meeting? This page explains it from the very beginning, in everyday language, one step at a time. You do not need any background in money or economics.

what_changed.headline: Monthly economic output remained flat in August, while financial markets adjusted following the October 28 rate hike.
items: Monthly GDP: Economic output was unchanged at 0.0% in August (Statistics Canada), following 0.0% in July, showing continued summer stagnation.
Market rates: The BoC policy rate stands at 2.50% and CORRA at 2.49%, following the October 28 increase, while the 2-year Government of Canada bond yield moved from 3.41% to 3.36% (October 29).
Canadian dollar: The exchange rate shifted slightly from C$1.3985 to C$1.3960 per US$1 (October 30).
Verdict stability: Our baseline view remains unchanged, with a 75% probability of a hold at 2.50% at the December 9 meeting.

verdict.headline: HOLD
verdict.sub: Keep the interest rate where it is, at 2.50%. After raising rates in October, the BoC is expected to pause and assess how higher borrowing costs and energy prices are working through the economy.
verdict.confidence_note: “Medium” means the BoC just acted to address persistent inflation risks, but incoming data on jobs and growth will dictate whether further tightening is needed.
verdict.short_version: Following its October 28 rate increase to 2.50%, the Bank of Canada is likely to pause at its December 9 meeting. Inflation remains near 3% and is expected to stay elevated through much of 2027, but weakening employment and new U.S. tariffs mean officials will want to evaluate incoming data before taking any further steps.
verdict.card_why: After raising the rate to 2.50% in October, the BoC is expected to hold steady while monitoring inflation persistence and job market softness.

why_steps.title: The BoC has one main job, and one main tool
why_steps.html: The Bank of Canada’s main job is to keep prices steady. Its target is that things should cost about 2% more each year, with a comfort zone of 1% to 3%. Unlike the U.S. Fed, it does not have a second official job about jobs, but it watches jobs closely because a weak job market usually pulls prices down later. Its main tool is its interest rate (officially the “overnight rate”), the cost of borrowing money between banks, which flows through to mortgages, car loans and savings accounts. Think of it like the pedals of a car. Raising the rate is pressing the brake: loans get more expensive, so people and companies borrow and spend less, and prices cool down. Cutting the rate is pressing the gas. Holding means keeping your foot where it is. Today the rate is 2.50%, following the October 28 increase. The BoC thinks a “neutral” rate, one that neither brakes nor speeds up the economy, is somewhere between 2.25% and 3.25% (July 2026 report). So today’s rate sits comfortably within that neutral range.

why_steps.title: Prices look high, but it is mostly gasoline
why_steps.html: Consumer prices (the CPI, or Consumer Price Index from Statistics Canada) were 3.1% higher in September than a year earlier, compared with 3.0% in August (StatCan). In simple terms: a basket of everyday things that cost $100 a year ago now costs about $103. The goal would be about $102. That puts Canada right at the top edge of the BoC’s 1%–3% comfort zone. In its October Monetary Policy Report, the BoC noted that inflation has been higher than anticipated and is projected to remain around 3% through much of 2027 before returning close to 2% by the middle of 2028 (BoC). Gasoline is up 27.8% in a year because of global energy shocks. Take gasoline out and prices are up only 2.2%. The BoC’s two favourite “core” measures, which strip out the most jumpy prices, are at 1.8% (CPI-trim) and 1.9% (CPI-median), right on target (BoC).

why_steps.title: Expensive oil cuts both ways for Canada
why_steps.html:
This is where Canada is different from the U.S. or Europe. Canada is a big oil producer and exporter. When oil is expensive, two things happen at once:
  • It hurts as a shopper. Families pay more at the pump and for heating, and trucking and flying cost more. That pushes the CPI up and leaves less money for other things.
  • It helps as a seller. Oil companies, workers and governments in producing provinces earn more. In August, energy exports rose 4.7% (StatCan), and in September Alberta added 23,000 jobs while the country as a whole lost jobs (StatCan).
  • An unusual twist: the loonie fell. Normally expensive oil lifts the Canadian dollar. This time one U.S. dollar went to about C$1.3960 (BoC), partly due to interest rate differences with the U.S. A weaker loonie makes imported goods dearer, adding to inflation risk.

why_steps.title: Jobs are weakening, and new U.S. tariffs add a worry
why_steps.html: Canada lost 41,700 jobs in August (revised) and 68,300 in September. Unemployment rose to 6.5%. The share of adults working or looking for work fell to 64.8%, partly because the population is ageing (StatCan). Pay is rising only 2.3% a year, slower than prices, so many workers are losing buying power. On top of that, new U.S. tariffs covering about 5% of Canada’s goods exports to the U.S. have created uncertainty. Governor Macklem noted that if they stay, growth could face headwinds. A weaker economy makes it harder for shops and firms to raise prices, which works against inflation.

why_steps.title: Weighing both sides

left: Headline inflation 3.1%, staying around 3% through 2027 (BoC forecast)
BoC raised rates in October to address upside risks
Weaker loonie and global rate differences
right: New U.S. tariffs and growth uncertainty
BoC expects to pause and assess impact

why_steps.html: Having delivered a 25 basis point hike in October to 2.50%, the BoC has pressed the brake to ensure energy-driven price pressures do not become permanent. However, with over 110,000 jobs lost across August and September and new U.S. tariffs weighing on growth, further immediate hikes are unlikely unless incoming inflation data proves stubborn. That is why we estimate a 75% Hold, 20% Raise, and 5% Cut for the December meeting.

why_steps.title: What the BoC has been saying
why_steps.html: In its October 28 press release and Monetary Policy Report, the BoC noted that “Inflation in Canada has been higher than anticipated and is projected to remain around 3% through much of 2027” before returning to 2% by mid-2028 (BoC). Governor Macklem emphasized during the press conference that while the economy's growth outlook has improved, uncertainty remains elevated. The October rate hike reflects the central bank's determination to keep inflation expectations anchored while watching incoming labor market and trade data.

why_steps.title: The road to the December 9 decision
why_steps.html: On Wednesday, December 9, the BoC announces its final rate decision of the year. Incoming reports on retail trade, monthly GDP, and the October Labour Force Survey will shape whether the Governing Council maintains the 2.50% rate or considers further adjustments.

timeline.title: The BoC cut its rate twice, to 2.25%
timeline.what: The BoC lowered its rate by 0.25 points in September (to 2.50%) and again in October (to 2.25%).
timeline.why: U.S. tariffs had hit Canada hard. The economy shrank in spring 2025, exports fell sharply, and unemployment reached 7.1%. Inflation looked close to the 2% target, so the BoC felt safe pressing the gas.
timeline.people: Variable-rate mortgages and lines of credit got a bit cheaper. Savings accounts paid a little less.
timeline.because: with the rate at 2.25%, the BoC held steady for nearly a year before a new energy shock arrived.

timeline.title: A pause: “about the right level”
timeline.what: The BoC held at 2.25% in December and January, viewing the rate as appropriate to keep inflation near 2%.
timeline.why: Growth was patchy and hiring was weak, but inflation was near target.
timeline.people: Loan and savings rates stayed about the same.
timeline.because: global energy markets soon introduced new inflationary pressures.

timeline.title: War in the Middle East: an energy shock
timeline.what: A conflict in the Middle East pushed up oil and gas prices. At its March 18 meeting the BoC held at 2.25% while noting increased global volatility.
timeline.why: Energy costs spiked, driving up headline inflation pressures.
timeline.people: Filling the car got more expensive within weeks.
timeline.because: inflation began climbing toward the upper edge of the comfort zone.

timeline.title: Oil peaks; the BoC draws a line
timeline.what: Oil peaked near US$120 a barrel in April. The BoC held at 2.25% and warned it would not let higher energy prices become persistent inflation.
timeline.why: Officials signaled they would act if fuel costs spread into wider prices.
timeline.because: the risk of pass-through inflation became the central bank's primary concern.

timeline.title: Holding, as jobs and growth recover
timeline.what: CPI rose to 3.2% in May. The BoC held at 2.25% at both summer meetings as growth rebounded in the spring.
timeline.why: Core inflation remained stable near 2%, keeping the trade-off balanced.
timeline.people: Jobs became a bit easier to find while price pressures at the pump persisted.
timeline.because: growth improved but energy volatility kept upside risks alive.

timeline.title: A strong spring, then new U.S. tariffs
timeline.what: The economy grew 0.8% in April–June. Trade talks with the U.S. broke down, resulting in new U.S. tariffs covering about 5% of Canadian goods exports.
timeline.because: tariffs threatened growth while energy prices pushed up inflation.

timeline.title: Held at 2.25%, with a firmer warning
timeline.what: The BoC held at 2.25% but warned that upside risks to inflation had increased.
timeline.why: Officials noted that prolonged high energy prices raised the likelihood of pass-through.
timeline.people: Bond yields rose as markets anticipated potential rate action.
timeline.because: incoming data through September set the stage for autumn policy tightening.

timeline.title: Underlying inflation steady, but jobs contract
timeline.what: Core inflation measures remained near 2% (CPI-trim 1.8%, CPI-median 1.9% in September), but employment fell sharply with 68,300 jobs lost in September and unemployment rising to 6.5%.
timeline.people: Workers faced a weaker hiring environment alongside rising living costs.
timeline.because: conflicting signals between sticky inflation and weak jobs created a delicate decision for October.

timeline.title: BoC raises the policy rate by 25 basis points to 2.50%
timeline.what: The Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate to 2.50% and published a new Monetary Policy Report projecting inflation to stay around 3% through much of 2027.
timeline.why: Higher-than-anticipated inflation and persistent energy pressures required a policy response to anchor expectations.
timeline.people: Borrowing costs on variable-rate mortgages and lines of credit increased.
timeline.because: with the rate now at 2.50%, the BoC enters a pause phase to evaluate incoming data ahead of December.

timeline.title: Assessing the new rate path ahead of December
timeline.what: Following the October hike, the BoC is holding steady at 2.50% while monitoring employment, retail sales, and tariff impacts.
timeline.why: The Governing Council wants to evaluate how the economy absorbs the October rate increase before considering further moves.
timeline.people: Borrowers and savers adjust to the 2.50% benchmark rate.
timeline.because: incoming reports through November will determine whether a hold or another hike is warranted in December.

choices.title: Hold: keep the rate at 2.50%
choices.meaning: the BoC pauses after its October hike to assess economic conditions and the impact of higher borrowing costs.
for: Recent rate hike: The BoC already raised rates to 2.50% in October to address persistent inflation risks.
Weakening jobs: Over 110,000 jobs were lost in August and September combined, and unemployment sits at 6.5%.
Core inflation on target: Core measures (CPI-trim 1.8%, CPI-median 1.9%) remain near the 2% goal.
New U.S. tariffs: Trade pressures create growth uncertainty that counsels caution.
against: Headline inflation is projected to stay around 3% through much of 2027 according to the new MPR.
Energy price volatility could continue to push up everyday costs.
choices.everyday: variable-rate mortgages, lines of credit, and savings rates would stay at their current levels following the October adjustment.

choices.title: Raise: up 0.25 points, to 2.75%
choices.meaning: the BoC tightens further if inflation proves stickier than expected through late 2026.
for: Headline inflation remains elevated and is projected to linger near 3% through much of 2027.
Global energy prices remain high and volatile.
A weaker loonie continues to add imported price pressures.
against: Recent job losses and rising unemployment argue against aggressive tightening.
The BoC typically prefers to pause and evaluate the impact after a rate increase.
choices.everyday: variable-rate mortgage payments and borrowing costs would rise further, while savers would earn higher returns.

choices.title: Cut: lower the rate
choices.meaning: the BoC reverses course to support growth if the economy experiences a severe downturn.
for: Significant job losses over two consecutive months point to underlying economic fragility.
Tariff escalation could severely impact Canadian exports.
against: Inflation is projected to remain around 3% through much of 2027, making rate cuts inappropriate.
The central bank just raised rates in October to combat inflation risks.
choices.everyday: borrowing costs would drop, but it would signal that economic conditions had deteriorated significantly.

change.lead: Our 75% / 20% / 5% forecast for December is based on today's data. Incoming economic reports will determine whether the BoC maintains its pause or considers further adjustments.
change.intro_title: Why upcoming data matters for December
change.intro: Now that the October 28 decision and Monetary Policy Report are complete, all eyes turn to incoming reports on trade, employment, and retail sales to see how the economy is responding to the 2.50% rate.

gdp_by_industry.why: Provides the first look at August economic output following summer stagnation.
gdp_by_industry.trigger: Strong growth → points toward potential future tightening. Weak growth → reinforces a hold.

merchandise_trade.why: Tracks September export performance and trade balance amid tariff concerns.
merchandise_trade.trigger: A widening trade surplus supports growth; trade contraction adds downside risk.

labour_force_survey.why: October jobs data will show whether employment stabilized after summer losses.
labour_force_survey.trigger: Job gains ease pressure on the BoC; further job losses strengthen the case for a prolonged hold.

market_participants_survey.why: Shows what financial professionals expect for upcoming rate decisions.
market_participants_survey.trigger: Shifts in market pricing will guide our probability assessments for December.

summary_of_deliberations_oct_28.why: Reveals the debate behind the October 28 rate hike and Governing Council views.
summary_of_deliberations_oct_28.trigger: Details on how close the vote was will clarify the path toward December.

change.other_title: Other things that could move our view
other: Oil and energy markets. Sustained high crude prices could keep headline inflation elevated, increasing pressure for further tightening.
U.S. tariffs and trade developments. Any escalation in trade tensions would weigh on growth and support a continued hold.
The Canadian dollar. Further depreciation of the loonie would increase import costs and add to price pressures.

report_card.one: Inflation is 3.1% and projected to remain around 3% through much of 2027, though core measures remain near 2%.
report_card.look: Consumer prices (CPI, up 3.1%), BoC core measures (CPI-trim 1.8%, CPI-median 1.9%), and inflation forecasts in the October MPR.
report_card.why: Headline inflation is at the top of the comfort zone, driven by energy costs, prompting the BoC to raise rates in October. However, underlying core inflation remains on target.
report_card.change: Headline inflation declining toward 2% or core measures rising above target.
report_card.matters: Inflation persistence was the primary driver of the October rate hike and remains key for future decisions.

report_card.one: Canada lost jobs in August and September, and unemployment rose to 6.5%.
report_card.look: Monthly employment change, unemployment rate, wage growth (2.3%), and participation rate (64.8%).
report_card.why: Employment fell 41,700 in August and 68,300 in September. Consecutive monthly losses signal a cooling labor market despite moderate wage growth.
report_card.change: Consistent job growth over multiple months → amber/green.
report_card.matters: Labor market weakness tempers the need for aggressive further rate hikes.

report_card.one: A strong spring rebound was followed by summer stagnation and tariff uncertainty.
report_card.look: Real GDP growth (0.8% in Q2), monthly GDP (0.0% in August), retail sales, and trade balance.
report_card.why: Economic momentum paused over the summer, and new U.S. tariffs pose ongoing risks to growth heading into late 2026.
report_card.change: Clear economic reacceleration → green; tariff-driven contraction → red.
report_card.matters: Growth uncertainty makes the BoC cautious about raising rates too aggressively.

report_card.one: Market borrowing costs have adjusted to the October rate hike, and the loonie trades near C$1.3960.
report_card.look: Government of Canada bond yields, CORRA overnight lending rate (2.49%), and the exchange rate.
report_card.why: Financial markets have absorbed the BoC's move to 2.50%, and CORRA operates effectively near the target rate while the loonie remains soft.
report_card.change: Significant shifts in bond yields or exchange rates.
report_card.matters: Market rates reflect ongoing expectations for the path of monetary policy.

consumer_price_index_cpi_all_items.what: Statistics Canada checks the prices of everyday goods and services compared with a year ago. A 3.1% rise means a $100 shopping basket now costs about $103.10.
consumer_price_index_cpi_all_items.why: this is the benchmark metric for the BoC's 2% target, currently sitting at the top of the 1%–3% comfort zone.

cpi_trim_boc_core_measure.what: the BoC removes extreme price swings (the top and bottom 20% of price changes) to measure underlying inflation trends.
cpi_trim_boc_core_measure.why: at 1.8%, it shows core price pressures remain contained despite high headline inflation.

cpi_median_boc_core_measure.what: the price change of the exact middle item in the consumer basket.
cpi_median_boc_core_measure.why: at 1.9%, it confirms underlying inflation is right near the 2% target.

cpi_without_food_and_energy_cpi_xfet.what: core consumer prices excluding food and energy.
cpi_without_food_and_energy_cpi_xfet.why: at 2.1%, it demonstrates that broader price pressures remain stable.

cpi_without_gasoline.why: at +2.2% vs a year ago, it illustrates how heavily headline inflation depends on energy costs.

gasoline_prices.what: what drivers pay at the pump.
gasoline_prices.why: at +27.8% vs a year ago, energy costs remain the primary driver of high headline inflation.

rent.why: shelter inflation is monitored closely as housing affordability remains a key focus.

food_from_stores.why: at +1.7% vs a year ago, grocery price growth has slowed notably.

businesses_inflation_expectations_1_an.what: business survey expectations of future inflation.
businesses_inflation_expectations_1_an.why: at 3% to 3.5%, expectations remain above target and are watched for persistence (manual snapshot).

employment_change.what: the monthly change in total employment from Statistics Canada.
employment_change.why: a drop of 68,300 in September highlights significant labor market cooling.

unemployment_rate.what: the share of the labor force actively looking for work without a job.
unemployment_rate.why: at 6.5%, unemployment has drifted higher over recent months.

average_hourly_wages.what: average hourly earnings growth for employees.
average_hourly_wages.why: at 2.3%, wage growth remains moderate and is not currently driving excessive inflation.

participation_rate.what: the share of the working-age population participating in the labor market.
participation_rate.why: at 64.8%, it reflects ongoing demographic shifts and an ageing population.

employment_rate.what: the share of the total adult population with a job.
employment_rate.why: at 60.6%, it confirms recent softness in labor market conditions.

public_sector_jobs.what: employment changes in public administration and government-funded services.
public_sector_jobs.why: down 70,000 in September, contributing significantly to the headline monthly contraction.

youth_unemployment_15_24.what: the unemployment rate for young workers aged 15 to 24.
youth_unemployment_15_24.why: at 13.0%, young job seekers face continued hiring challenges.

job_vacancies.what: open positions employers are trying to fill.
job_vacancies.why: stands at 510,200 (rate 2.8%) from Q2 2026 data (manual snapshot).

real_gdp_growth_spring.what: economic growth measured by gross domestic product.
real_gdp_growth_spring.why: at 0.8% in Q2 2026, it marked a solid rebound from earlier quarters (old status).

monthly_gdp.why: at 0.0% in August 2026, economic momentum paused over the summer.

retail_sales.what: total retail sales at Canadian stores.
retail_sales.why: up 1.2% in August 2026, showing a temporary pickup in consumer demand.

merchandise_trade_balance.what: the difference between the value of goods exported and imported.
merchandise_trade_balance.why: stands at $4.2 billion for August 2026, supported by strong energy exports.

household_saving_rate.what: the share of disposable income households save.
household_saving_rate.why: at 3.7% in Q2 2026, it leaves households with a modest financial buffer.

building_permits.what: total value of construction permits approved by municipalities.
building_permits.why: at $13.6 billion in August 2026, pointing to mixed construction activity.

boc_growth_forecast_for_2026.what: the central bank's annual growth forecast.
boc_growth_forecast_for_2026.why: at 0.7% in the July report, it underscores expectations for a subdued economic year (manual snapshot).

boc_policy_rate_overnight_rate_target.what: the BoC's target interest rate for overnight loans between banks.
boc_policy_rate_overnight_rate_target.why: at 2.50% following the October 28 hike, it serves as the benchmark borrowing cost for the economy.

corra_overnight_lending_rate.what: the Canadian Overnight Repo Rate Average, representing actual overnight bank lending costs.
corra_overnight_lending_rate.why: at 2.49%, it operates effectively near the policy target.

2_year_government_of_canada_bond.what: government borrowing costs for a two-year term.
2_year_government_of_canada_bond.why: at 3.36%, it reflects investor expectations for monetary policy.

5_year_government_of_canada_bond.what: government borrowing costs for a five-year term.
5_year_government_of_canada_bond.why: at 3.58%, it influences fixed mortgage rates for households.

10_year_government_of_canada_bond.what: government borrowing costs for a ten-year term.
10_year_government_of_canada_bond.why: at 3.84%, higher long-term yields help cool borrowing independently.

canadian_dollar_us_1_in_c.what: the exchange rate between the Canadian dollar and the U.S. dollar.
canadian_dollar_us_1_in_c.why: at C$1.3960, a softer loonie makes imported goods dearer, adding slight price pressure.

market_forecasters_expected_boc_rate_p.what: survey of financial market professionals regarding expected BoC rates.
market_forecasters_expected_boc_rate_p.why: indicates rate expectations over coming quarters (manual snapshot from June survey).

boc_estimate_of_the_neutral_rate.what: the theoretical interest rate that neither stimulates nor slows the economy.
boc_estimate_of_the_neutral_rate.why: estimated at 2.25% to 3.25% (July 2026 report, manual snapshot).

oil_price_wti_crude.what: North American crude oil benchmark price.
oil_price_wti_crude.why: at US$96.24 a barrel, it drives energy costs and export earnings (manual snapshot).

oil_price_brent_crude.why: at US$125.44 a barrel, global energy prices remain elevated (manual snapshot).

u_s_federal_reserve_rate.what: the main U.S. central bank interest rate.
u_s_federal_reserve_rate.why: at 3.75% – 4.00%, international rate differences affect exchange rates and trade (manual snapshot).

european_central_bank_deposit_rate.what: the main interest rate for the euro area.
european_central_bank_deposit_rate.why: at 2.50%, it shows global peers facing similar conditions (manual snapshot).

average_u_s_tariff_on_canadian_goods.what: average tariff rate applied by the U.S. on Canadian goods.
average_u_s_tariff_on_canadian_goods.why: estimated at 5.0% as of July 2026 assumptions (manual snapshot).

Why it matters: Provides ongoing central bank research and economic commentary from leadership.

said.n: Press Conference: Monetary Policy Report – October 2026
said.v: MPR and press conference following rate hike
w: What it said: The Bank of Canada raised the policy rate by 25 basis points to 2½% and published its October Monetary Policy Report.
Why it matters: Sets out the updated official economic forecast showing inflation staying around 3% through much of 2027.
What it said: “Inflation in Canada has been higher than anticipated and is projected to remain around 3% through much of 2027. It then returns close to 2% by the middle of 2028.”
Why it matters: Explains the rationale behind the October rate increase to 2.50% to address persistent inflation risks.
What it said: “the upside risks to inflation have increased, while new tariffs make growth prospects more uncertain”, and the BoC “is prepared to adjust monetary policy as needed.”
Why it matters: Formally signaled that upside inflation risks were growing.

said.v: Response “could” be needed if inflation spreads
w: What it said: members agreed “the risk that inflation spreads to other goods and services had risen”, and that spreading “could require a monetary policy response to prevent broad-based inflation from setting in.”
Why it matters: Outlined the central bank's trigger for raising rates.

said.v: “the risk that inflation broadens and becomes more persistent has increased.”
w: What he said: “if oil prices stay near $100 per barrel, we would expect inflation to edge up in the coming months”, but “We don’t want to raise our policy rate and restrain growth if inflationary pressures are contained.”
Why it matters: Highlighted the balancing act between energy-driven inflation and softening growth.
What she said: housing affordability is complex, interest rates are too blunt a tool for it, and other factors drive the market beyond what monetary policy alone can touch.
Why it matters: Reminds us that broader structural issues influence housing alongside borrowing costs.

gaps: Upcoming indicator releases such as September international merchandise trade will arrive shortly. Why it matters: incoming data will refine trade and economic momentum after the October rate decision.

Market-implied rate odds. Official market pricing for December meeting probabilities was not available; we rely on our qualitative assessment. Why it matters: exact market consensus pricing cannot be directly compared against our probability estimates.

Manual snapshots and surveys. Several indicators (such as business expectations and neutral rate estimates) rely on periodic manual releases rather than daily feeds. Why it matters: these figures represent historical survey intervals rather than real-time data.

group_intros.prices: These numbers tell us how fast things are getting more expensive. The BoC’s goal is 2% a year for total CPI, inside a 1%–3% comfort zone. It uses “core” measures, which remove the jumpiest prices, to see the underlying trend.
group_intros.jobs: These numbers show whether people can find and keep work. Jobs are not the BoC’s official target, but a weak job market usually means lower inflation later, so it weighs heavily on the decision.
group_intros.growth: These numbers show how fast the economy is growing and whether people are still spending. A strong economy can handle higher interest rates. A weak one cannot.
group_intros.rates: These numbers show the BoC’s own rate and the rates set by investors in financial markets. Market rates often move before the BoC does, because investors try to guess its next step.
group_intros.said: BoC officials often hint at what they will do next. Reading their words carefully is one of the best ways to guess the next decision.
group_intros.global: Canada’s economy depends heavily on what happens elsewhere, especially oil prices, U.S. trade policy and what other central banks do.

copy.story_intro: This is the story of the past year, in order. Each step explains what happened, why it happened, and what it meant for ordinary people. The line at the bottom of each step (“Because of this…”) shows how it led to the next step, so you can follow cause and effect from start to finish.
copy.choices_intro: At every meeting the BoC has three options. Below we explain what each one would mean, why it could happen, why it might not, and what it would mean in everyday life. Analysis · our judgement
copy.report_intro: Think of this as a school report for the economy in four subjects. Green means healthy. Yellow means mixed, keep watching. Red means a problem the central bank must fix. Each grade is also written in words, so you do not need to see the color. Analysis
copy.gaps_intro: Good research is honest about its blind spots. Here is what is missing, delayed or unverified, and why it matters.
copy.numbers_intro: Every number we used, grouped by topic. For each one you will see the latest value, the period it covers, when it was published, the previous value, where it came from, and, most importantly, a plain explanation of what it is and why it matters. Tap a group to open or close it. Observed facts

live_before.html: The numbers on this page are a snapshot taken on October 14, 2026. If you want to see whether anything has changed since then, you can try loading the newest values from FRED, a free public data service run by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Note: FRED does not carry an up-to-date Canadian CPI series (its OECD copy stops in March 2025), so for prices use Statistics Canada and the BoC directly. Some FRED series below are monthly averages or arrive with a delay, so they may differ slightly from our daily figures.

How it works: FRED gives anyone a free “API key”, a code that works like a library card for its data. Paste your key below and press Refresh. The newest values appear in a separate table, next to our snapshot values so you can compare. The rest of this page stays exactly as it is.
Privacy: your key is saved only in this browser, on this device, and is sent only to FRED. Press “Forget key” to remove it. Get a free key at fred.stlouisfed.org.

live_after.html: Good to know: FRED often does not allow web pages to request its data directly, so many browsers will block this. If that happens, you will see a clear message and nothing on the page will change. You can always check the same numbers yourself on the FRED website.

summary.headline: Monthly economic output remained flat in August, while financial markets adjusted following the October 28 rate hike.
items: Monthly GDP: Economic output was unchanged at 0.0% in August (Statistics Canada), following 0.0% in July, showing continued summer stagnation.
Market rates: The BoC policy rate stands at 2.50% and CORRA at 2.49%, following the October 28 increase, while the 2-year Government of Canada bond yield moved from 3.41% to 3.36% (October 29).
Canadian dollar: The exchange rate shifted slightly from C$1.3985 to C$1.3960 per US$1 (October 30).
Verdict stability: Our baseline view remains unchanged, with a 75% probability of a hold at 2.50% at the December 9 meeting.

summary.headline: No major rate decision or policy announcement occurred since the October 28 rate hike, with financial markets and incoming data monitored ahead of December.
items: Market rates: The 2-year Government of Canada bond yield edged up slightly from 3.36% to 3.41% (October 28), and the 5-year yield moved from 3.57% to 3.62% (October 28).
Canadian dollar: The exchange rate shifted from C$1.4036 to C$1.3985 per US$1 (October 29).
Verdict stability: Our baseline view remains unchanged, with a 75% probability of a hold at 2.50% at the December 9 meeting.

summary.headline: The Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate by 25 basis points to 2.50% on October 28, 2026, alongside a new Monetary Policy Report.
items: Rate decision: The BoC raised the policy interest rate from 2.25% to 2.50% (October 28).

Monetary Policy Report: The BoC published its updated forecast, noting that inflation has been higher than anticipated and is projected to remain around 3% through much of 2027 before returning close to 2% by the middle of 2028.
Verdict update: With the October rate hike completed, our verdict shifts to the next meeting on December 9, 2026, where a hold at 2.50% is currently most likely.
